title: Visual Scaffolds Reveal What VLM Benchmarks Measure
hook: Redraw the same spatial puzzle to make its structure legible and accuracy jumps up to 34 points — so was the benchmark ever testing reasoning?
key_points: VLM failures often mix two things: grounding the image, and reasoning over what was grounded.
The study varies only visual presentation on SPaRC, a grid-based visual spatial planning benchmark.
Lightweight input-side scaffolds keep the task in the visual modality but make spatial structure more accessible.
Scaffolds improved accuracy by up to 34.0 percentage points across multiple VLMs.
They also complement GRPO training: up to 4.6 extra points, versus near-zero gains on the original visual input.
Error analysis ties the gains to fewer grounding errors; rule reasoning stays hard either way.
content_html: When a vision-language model flubs a spatial puzzle, it is rarely clear whether it misread the picture or reasoned badly about what it read. Lars Benedikt Kaesberg and colleagues isolate the first factor on SPaRC, a grid-based visual spatial planning benchmark, by adding lightweight input-side scaffolds — changes to how the task is drawn that leave the reasoning problem identical and keep everything in the visual modality.
extra_html: Across several VLMs, the scaffolds lift accuracy by as much as 34.0 percentage points, and they stack with GRPO-based training in a way the original inputs do not: up to 4.6 further points, where the unscaffolded setting yields near zero. Analyses of both end-to-end solving and object detection tie the improvement to fewer grounding errors, while rule reasoning stays comparatively stubborn. The authors' conclusion is a methodological one — visual presentation decides whether a multimodal benchmark is measuring grounded perception, downstream reasoning, or an untangled mixture. Paper on arXiv.

related.title: MentalThink: Reasoning Through Rendered SVG Sketches
related.hook: Instead of imagining a scene in words, this model sketches it — generating SVG code, rendering it, and looking at the result to check its own spatial reasoning.

related.title: Seeing Red, Thinking Bad: Color Bias in VLMs
related.hook: Render the same sentence with the positive words in green and a vision-language model reads it more positively. The text didn't change — only its styling did.

flashcards.prompt: What is a 'visual scaffold' in this paper?
flashcards.back_html: A lightweight change to the input image that keeps the task visual but makes its spatial structure more accessible — the underlying reasoning problem is unchanged.

flashcards.prompt: What do the scaffolding results imply about VLM spatial-reasoning benchmarks?

choices.text: Scores partly measure visual grounding, so a benchmark's presentation determines what it actually tests
VLMs cannot do spatial reasoning at all
Grid-based benchmarks are equivalent to text-based ones

flashcards.explanation_html: Since presentation alone moved accuracy by up to 34 points and the gains trace to fewer grounding errors, the benchmark was scoring perception and reasoning together.

flashcards.prompt: How did scaffolds interact with GRPO-based training?
flashcards.back_html: They complemented it: up to 4.6 additional accuracy points on scaffolded input, versus near-zero gains from the same training on the original visual input.
